transcript:
Meeting header:
14:00 PST • 2027-11-03 • 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Devon Park (Redwood SE), Karen Ito (Silverpine SRE), Raj Patel (CTO), Lisa Monroe (PM), Tom Reyes (Platform)

Summary: quick run through of console request tracing and how to stitch logs -> traces -> model calls, then demo of error analysis flow and KV cache fallback visualization.

00:00 Maya: okay everyone thanks for joining, um we wanted to — we have about 45 minutes so we'll focus the first half on trace stitching and then dig into the error flow that Karen sent over, is that still the right plan?
00:12 Karen: yeah that sounds good. we flagged the recommendation 503s that happen during peak traffic, and there's some inconsistent latencies on the frontend when the model falls back.
00:20 Devon: perfect been looking at the sample you sent, there's a couple places where the request ID is not propagated through the queue worker so the console can't stitch the downstream model call back to the user request — we'll demo the trace correlator and what to look for.
00:37 Raj: quick ask -- we're doing private deploy for compliance, so we'll want to see how the request traces look when the control plane is out of band, anything extra we need to know?
00:48 Maya: good point — we'll cover the VPC options and the control plane telemetry and what stays customer-side.

03:05 Devon: ok jumping into the console — first thing is the request inspector, you can search by request id, user id, or route. if a request isn't stitched you'll see an orphaned model call with no parent. here's an example from your logs, request id xyz-987 showed a model call for gpt-retail-v2 at 11:39 but no parent event. sometimes that's a header drop in the worker.
03:36 Lisa: is that something that could happen in our load balancer? we do some header rewriting for tracking.
03:45 Devon: yes that can cause it — the console has header propagation checks and a quick rule is to ensure x-redwood-request-id (or whatever header you're using) is on the passthrough. also we show a waterfall with timestamps so you can see exactly where the gap is.

07:10 Maya: side note-- the KV cache miss pattern you described earlier, that's often visible as an extra model token spike in the trace. Devon, can you show that?
07:20 Devon: yeah so here, when KV cache misses we show an upstream cache lookup event then the model call with extra tokens and increased latency; the console annotates it as "cache-miss" with a red flag. see 12:14 on this trace. note: transcription of event names in the ui might say "kv chase" in older builds, so if you see odd labels don't panic.
07:45 Tom: we've also seen fallback routing to a cheaper model cause different output shapes which breaks downstream parser, will that show up?
07:54 Devon: it should — we surface the model variant in the trace and the console can diff the output shape across rollouts. that helps you see when a fallback produced truncated JSON or different keys.

11:02 Karen: here's the failing trace we uploaded — the user request times out then we see a cascade: the worker retries three times then the router falls back to lower tier model and returns 502 at the api gateway. can you replay that?
11:15 Devon: yep loading it now. so i see the initial request, the queue delay is 420 ms, then a worker restart at 11:23:06 which lost the request id header. see that null parent? that's the orphan. then two serial retries. retries are happening client-side so they spawn new request ids which prevents auto-aggregation in the console.
11:45 Raj: hmm so the retries are inflating our token cost, and also obfuscating true latency. is there a way to collapse retries into a single logical request for metrics?
11:55 Devon: we have a logical-operation tag you can enable in the agent — it groups retries by original request fingerprint, we can flip that in your deploy during the POC. caveat: it requires a small client-side change to propagate the original id in x-redwood-original-id.
12:20 Lisa: any privacy or compliance concern with that header?
12:28 Maya: it's just an opaque id, no PII. we encrypt at rest and the control plane doesn't keep payloads in hosted by default; since you're looking at private VPC, all telemetry stays in your network unless you opt into forwarding.

15:00 Devon: switching to the error-analysis panel: you can filter by error type, model, route. we attach the full request payload snapshot (scrubbed) and the model response. note: transcriptions can be imperfect so some model output tokens may be redacted in the export.
15:24 Karen: in one of the examples the model returned a malformed JSON — can the console highlight the exact token index where parsing failed?
15:33 Devon: yes we show a diff and a parser fail line number if your parser returns an error message; if not, we have heuristics to approximate the index by attempting a minimal parse. it won't be perfect but it's often enough to find the root cause.

19:02 Maya: on deployment options — for private/vpc we give you two modes: customer-managed control plane, or a hybrid where telemetry summaries (not payloads) are optionally posted to Redwood for visibility. Raj wanted to confirm that if we do customer-managed, you still get the same console UX?
19:20 Raj: UX parity is important — we don't want different tooling for devs vs prod.
19:27 Maya: parity is the goal; the console in your VPC will have the same trace viewer but the control plane endpoints are internal. some advanced features like cross-customer benchmarking won't be available.

22:40 Devon: performance notes: we recommend sticky routing for low-latency routes and continuous batching for high-throughput. sticky routing reduces KV cache invalidation but can increase tail latency under churn. here's the tradeoff: if your 95th is critical keep sticky and add capacity; if cost is primary we can relax it and tune batching.
23:08 Tom: we've got a hard 120ms p95 target for interactive recommendations, our current is ~200ms under load. can Redwood meet 120?
23:20 Devon: depends on model and quantization; for our gpt-retail with int8 quant it can hit ~80-100ms p95 on A100-class hosts for 512 token windows. but with network hops and your worker queue delays you may see higher numbers; that's why the benchmark with your payloads is critical.

26:50 Karen: about logs — we wanted to keep request logs for 90 days internally. what are retention constraints with private deploy?
26:58 Maya: in private deployments retention is your call — the console UI can query from your S3/obj store; Redwood hosted retains 30 days by default and we have add-ons for longer. for PII we recommend field-level scrubbing at ingestion.

29:40 Devon: demoing the trace correlator: here I click the orphaned model call and use "stitch by time window" to surface potential parents. it's heuristic-based: if header id missing we'll look +-500ms and match on user agent and route. sometimes you'll get false positives — that's why we show confidence score.
30:10 Lisa: that heuristic could be noisy during peak, do you expose the confidence threshold?
30:18 Devon: yes you can tune it in advanced settings per route, and export matches to a CSV for large-scale audit.

33:05 Maya: quick question — are you planning to drive rollouts from the console or via your infra pipeline?
33:12 Raj: infra pipeline for staging->prod but devs might use console for quick experiments.
33:18 Maya: ok for that we recommend RBAC tightness: redact config toggles to only SRE and Platform, and use canary policies so console rollouts don't override infra policies.

36:25 Devon: now the replay tool — this is useful for reproducing the failing request locally. you can replay the exact model call (scrubbed) to a sandbox environment with deterministic seeds. note: replay won't reproduce transient network failures in your worker, but it will show model-side behavior.
36:50 Tom: can replay target a local docker image for our in-house model?
36:56 Devon: yes, you can point the replay to any model endpoint that's compatible and the console will remap the model tag. there's a small adapter shim we include in the POC bundle.

40:10 Karen: about cost visibility — we need token-level cost attribution per request for chargeback, can we export that?
40:18 Maya: yes console exposes token and op-level cost breakdowns per request and per route. if you're private, the accounting runs in your cluster and we provide the CSV and API to pull it.

42:45 Raj: to confirm next steps: we'll get logs and SSO metadata; Redwood runs benchmark; and then we do POC kick-off. timeline?
42:55 Maya: aiming to start POC week of 2027-11-15 assuming logs and security docs land this week. Devon will run the earlier benchmark and share results.

45:10 Devon: small note, the sample you sent had some garbled agent names (the worker client had an older SDK) — for accurate traces please upgrade to our 1.8 agent, it includes better header propagation and logical-operation grouping.
45:26 Tom: yep we can schedule the SDK upgrade with our ops team.

46:05 Maya: awesome, i'll email the SOC2 and network sketches after this. thanks everyone for the time. any last questions?
46:15 Lisa: none from me.
46:20 Karen: no, thanks, useful session.
46:24 Maya: great, bye all.
